content: The guidelines for managing advanced HIV disease and the rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), published in July 2017 by the World Health Organization (WHO), provide detailed recommendations for addressing the challenges faced by patients presenting with advanced stages of HIV. These guidelines are available under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations of the work must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the content or accuracy of the translation, and the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guidelines emphasize that a significant proportion of HIV-positive patients continue to present to healthcare services at an advanced stage of the disease, despite global progress in scaling up ART access and initiating treatment at higher CD4 cell counts. Advanced HIV disease is defined by WHO as a CD4 count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of WHO Clinical Stage 3 or 4 defining illnesses. Mortality rates remain high among these patients, even within the first three months of ART initiation, due to co-infections such as tuberculosis (TB), cryptococcal meningitis, severe bacterial infections, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Approximately 25% of patients globally begin ART with a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³, with sub-Saharan Africa facing particularly significant challenges in addressing advanced HIV disease. Studies from the region indicate that a substantial proportion of patients initiate ART with critically low CD4 counts, highlighting barriers to timely presentation, diagnosis, and linkage to care. These barriers must be addressed to maximize the population-level benefits of ART. WHO guidelines recommend several interventions in addition to ART to reduce mortality and morbidity in patients with advanced HIV disease. These include isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) to prevent TB, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, screening for cryptococcal disease in adults with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³ in high-prevalence settings, and TB screening using urine lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LAM) assays. Recent studies have explored the potential of enhanced intervention packages, which include infection prophylaxis, screening, and other care elements delivered together, to improve outcomes in this patient population. The systematic review conducted to inform these guidelines included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving HIV-positive patients with advanced disease, defined as a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ and/or WHO Stage 3 or 4 disease. The interventions studied were packages of two or more components designed to reduce mortality and severe morbidity. Outcomes analyzed included all-cause mortality, incident morbidity, hospitalizations, serious adverse events, CD4 cell gain, and ART adherence. The review followed PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews and included searches of databases and conference proceedings up to September 2016. Only two open-label RCTs met the inclusion criteria, and the certainty of the evidence was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool and the GRADE framework. These tools evaluated the quality of evidence and the risk of bias in the included studies, ensuring that the recommendations are based on robust and reliable data.
